t: Good morning, it's the Ah Beng AI Daily Brief for Sunday, September thirteenth. And today is all about one question: what would you build now that you never would have before?
Right. Because GPT-6 Astra dropped a week ago, and honestly, people are confused. It's the smartest and strangest model yet.
Strangest how?
Power users describe it as the smartest and dumbest model they've ever worked with. Mood swings. Absurd shortcuts to something that technically works.
And here's the kicker — OpenCode's team partially went back to GPT-56 Sol, the older model, because their effective spend on Astra roughly doubled.
Doubled? For coding it's tough to justify. Advanced coders are quietly retreating to older models.
But step outside your day job and the picture flips. In familiar use cases, Astra's improvements aren't even noticeable. Sometimes it feels like a step back.
Yet in stuff that was never part of your job — video editing, 3D design, one-shot 3D games — it's beyond anything before it.
So today's one idea: the new models' value is in things you've never considered. Which means you need thought starters, not benchmarks.
And that's the whole frame — efficiency AI versus opportunity AI. Efficiency AI does your existing work better. Faster, cheaper.
Opportunity AI unlocks entirely new opportunities. And here's the thing — that's usually been a mindset distinction, not a difference in the models themselves.
Astra is one of the first models where the difference is real. It actually dances inside that divide.
Now, efficiency AI is not the enemy. It's the foundation of most AI use and most initial value.
Mm.
But here's what the winners see: efficiency gains reset expectations for everyone. The companies chasing new opportunities — even ones orthogonal to what they do today — race out ahead.
So how do you actually find opportunities? You ask someone to go find AI opportunities and you get... a blank page.
Every time. Nobody walks around with a complete inventory of things they might make. We all carry a smaller inventory shaped by our job, our tools, and what people around us do.
Even NLW's own opportunity use cases — like the pipeline that turns episodes into shareable chunks — came from stumbling and experimenting, not planning.
And the shortcut? Many of these opportunities aren't totally novel. They're things other people can already do that you couldn't.
So steal. Look at what people in different roles are doing that you think is really cool, and bring it into your own work.
Okay, thought starters. Number one: make marketing people can play.
Marketing has been visual, print, video. AI opens up interactivity. Some of the most exciting first Astra experiments were literally games.
So put games inside of work. Instead of telling someone a place rewards curiosity, give them a small mystery that makes them curious.
A game implicates the audience's agency. They're not a receiver anymore.
And a game's rules can carry your sales argument. Say you're a consultant pitching cross-team decision-making — sounds abstract, right?
So give the prospect a five-minute fictional product launch. Sales promises a date, product finds a dependency, support lacks information.
The prospect encounters the exact problem your service solves — and gets language for it. That's the pitch.
Now, most games fail. Game design is still hard — way more games are released than ever become popular, even from professionals.

But that's not the point. Brands were constrained by development resources before. Now a solopreneur can experiment this weekend. Opportunity AI doesn't guarantee hits — it lowers the cost of the attempt.
Thought starter two: build your own video production pipeline. Fun fact — the Daily Brief's clips aren't made by Opus or any clipping product.
They come from a custom-built, Claude-run pipeline that ingests the script and raw video and produces the output. These models may democratize video the way coding agents democratized software.
And there's homework. Write a sixty-second educational marketing script with AI. Record it on your phone.
Then hand the video to Codex or Claude Code. Ask for a visual motif, transitions, layered graphics, and a full production pipeline — so all you do is drop in source video.
One round of feedback. Then ask yourself: does this lower the barrier enough that video becomes a real tool for me?
Thought starter three: product demos organized by the buyer's curiosity.
A sales presentation has to pick one order. But different buyers arrive with different questions.
An exploratory demo organizes itself around actions — open this, isolate that component, inspect the result. The visitor's question determines the path.
The question to ask: what do customers need to inspect for themselves before your product makes sense?
Thought starter four, and this one's big: proposals clients can shape.
Every proposal already contains an invisible model — assumptions about work, parallelism, resources, timing.
Instead of handing over one selected plan, expose parts of that model. We want it sooner becomes we can finish sooner if the team attends more often.
Clients explore the trade-offs themselves, without every alternative becoming a new request for you to interpret.
And that's efficiency and opportunity AI in one. It radically cuts the latency of back-and-forth in every negotiation.
It'll become completely de rigueur. We'll struggle to remember doing it any other way.
Thought starter five: build simulators for business decisions. We need another hire — that one sentence hides so many disagreements.
Right. Is the process too slow? Is work unevenly distributed? Are you expecting a demand surge? People argue about conclusions while imagining totally different starting conditions.
A simulator forces you to specify those conditions. Each assumption's consequence becomes something you can inspect — does the decision hold if demand rises more slowly?
And notice the pattern underneath: interactive proposals, decision simulators — they're all what-if machines. What if we did this? What trade-offs follow?
Making that reasoning manipulable is a core opportunity-AI move.

Then there's 3D. Some of the first genuine Astra excitement came from people driving Blender — 3D walkthroughs of Zillow houses, learning experiences where rotating a digital object changes how you learn.
3D is a big part of what makes Astra unique, and one of the best places to spend your experimentation time.
Thought starter seven: turn customer stories into mini documentaries. You already have the raw material — interviews, project reviews, recordings, screenshots.
An interview explains why a situation mattered. A recording shows what changed. A film combines them — the audience recognizes the problem, inspects the invention, judges the outcome.
First pass: dump the raw assets into Claude Code or Codex and let it one-shot the architecture. Just to feel the capability.
Thought starter eight: simulate the situation before it's real. The hardest part of training is creating space to exercise judgment — difficult customers, hard conversations with management.
Simulation-style environments give immediate feedback on judgment, midstream. This will likely become an entire category of professional development.

Thought starter nine: treat physical conditions as something you can design. 3D modeling makes physical products prototypable — or something abstract, like a teacher's object with removable pieces that makes a difficult relationship tangible.
Even something like acoustic panels shaped by a studio's own measurements.
And the last one — thought starter twelve: your expertise as a product.
Expert help is a conversation. But inside it you're gathering context, recognizing patterns, ruling out attractive-but-wrong options, deciding what someone is ready for.
Give a specific part of that judgment a form people can work through themselves. It scales you — works for teammates as much as clients.
And it doubles as efficiency AI wherever you repeat the same things to different people.
So the takeaway: efficiency and opportunity AI aren't at war. Several of these ideas turn out to be both at once.
The point of the thought starters is simple — you don't have to know in advance what your opportunity looks like.
Astra can do novel things. Your job is to stumble into the ones that matter for you. That's the brief — see you tomorrow.
See you tomorrow.
